text: Mercier Philip Cunningham (April 16, 1919 – July 26, 2009) was an American dancer and choreographer who led American modern dance for over 50 years. He frequently collaborated with artists from various disciplines, including musicians John Cage, David Tudor, Brian Eno, and visual artists Robert Rauschenberg, Bruce Nauman, Andy Warhol, Roy Lichtenstein, Frank Stella, and Jasper Johns, as well as fashion designer Rei Kawakubo; these collaborations had a significant impact on avant-garde art. As a choreographer, teacher, and leader of the Merce Cunningham Dance Company (MCDC), he profoundly influenced modern dance, with many of his former students forming their own companies, such as Paul Taylor, Remy Charlip, Viola Farber, Charles Moulton, Karole Armitage, Deborah Hay, Robert Kovich, Foofwa d'Imobilité, Kimberly Bartosik, Flo Ankah, Jan Van Dyke, Jonah Bokaer, and Alice Reyes. Cunningham earned major artistic honors, including the National Medal of Arts, the MacArthur Fellowship, Japan's Praemium Imperiale, and a British Laurence Olivier Award, and was named Officier of the Légion d'honneur in France. His life and artistic vision have been explored in numerous books, films, and exhibitions, and his works have been presented by groups such as the Paris Opéra Ballet, New York City Ballet, American Ballet Theatre, White Oak Dance Project, and London's Rambert Dance Company. Born in Centralia, Washington, in 1919 as the second of three sons, Cunningham first experienced dance through a tap class with Mrs. Maude Barrett, whose emphasis on precise musical timing shaped his understanding of musicality. He studied acting at the Cornish College of the Arts in Seattle from 1937 to 1939 but found drama too limiting, favoring dance’s ambiguous and exploratory nature. Martha Graham saw him dance and invited him to join her company, where he performed as a soloist from 1939 to 1945. In April 1944, he presented his first solo concert in New York with composer John Cage, who became his lifelong romantic partner and frequent collaborator until Cage's death in 1992. In 1953, while teaching at Black Mountain College, he formed the Merce Cunningham Dance Company. The original company included dancers Carolyn Brown, Viola Farber, Marianne Preger-Simon, Paul Taylor, and Remy Charlip, and musicians John Cage and David Tudor. In 1964, the Cunningham Dance Foundation was established to support his work. MCDC made its first international tour in 1964, visiting Europe and Asia. From 1971 until its dissolution in 2012, the company was based in the Westbeth Artists Community in the West Village, where Cunningham lived at 107 Bank Street with John Cage. On July 20, 1999, Cunningham and Mikhail Baryshnikov performed together at the New York State Theater for his 80th birthday. In its later years, MCDC had a two-year residency at Dia Beacon, performing Events—site-specific choreographic works—in galleries designed by Richard Serra, Dan Flavin, and Sol LeWitt. In 2007, MCDC premiered XOVER, Cunningham's final collaboration with Rauschenberg, at Dartmouth College. In 2009, MCDC premiered Cunningham's newest work, Nearly Ninety, at the Brooklyn Academy of Music to mark his 90th birthday. The company concluded its farewell tour on December 31, 2011, at the Park Avenue Armory. Cunningham choreographed more than 200 dances and over 800 Events. In 1963, he joined with Cage to create the Walker Art Center's first performance, beginning a 25-year collaborative relationship. He often used the I Ching to determine the sequence of his dances, and dancers were frequently not informed of the order until the night of the performance. He performed as a dancer in his company into the early 1990s. In 1968, he published Changes: Notes on Choreography, edited by Francis Starr. A mural in Washington Hall at Centralia College honors him. Cunningham valued the process over the product and used chance procedures, such as coin tosses or playing cards, to determine movement sequences, as seen in Suite by Chance (1953), Field Dances (1963), and Canfield (1969). He believed dance did not need a beginning, middle, or end and emphasized non-representational choreography that focused on movement without narrative or emotional content. In Sixteen Dances for Soloist and Company of Three (1951), indeterminacy was first used, with the sequence of sections changing per performance. In Story (1963), dancers selected costumes and sets from second-hand clothes and new designs by Rauschenberg. Cunningham was a pioneer in applying new technologies to the arts, beginning film experiments in the 1970s and choreographing with computer programs like LifeForms (after 1991) and DanceForms, which used avatars for choreography. He created Westbeth (1974) in collaboration with filmmaker Charles Atlas and explored motion capture with Paul Kaiser and Shelley Eshkar, producing Hand-drawn Spaces (1998) and the live dance BIPED. In 2008, he released Loops, a choreography for the hands as motion-capture data under a Creative Commons license, which became the basis for an open-source collaboration with The OpenEnded Group. In 2009, he launched the behind-the-scenes webcast Mondays with Merce. His choreography eliminated the traditional front-and-center stage focus, allowing movement anywhere on the stage and viewing from any angle, emphasizing randomness and arbitrariness as positive qualities. In June 2009, the Cunningham Dance Foundation announced the Legacy Plan, a first-of-its-kind roadmap for the future of MCDC, outlining a comprehensive digital documentation and preservation program to ensure future study and performance of his works. The plan established the Merce Cunningham Trust as the custodian of his dances for licensing, with detailed records prepared by associates to allow authentic productions by other companies. It also included a final international tour and the eventual closure of the Cunningham Dance Foundation and MCDC, with all assets transferred to the Trust. From Cunningham's death at age 90 through the board's last meeting in 2012, the plan implemented his wish for a worldwide legacy tour followed by closure. The final performance of MCDC was on December 31, 2011, at the Park Avenue Armory. The board's final meeting was held on March 15, 2012, in Cunningham's studio at the top of the Westbeth building. Numerous exhibitions have honored his work, including Invention: Merce Cunningham & Collaborators at the New York Public Library for the Performing Arts (closed October 13, 2007), Merce Cunningham: Dancing on the Cutting Edge at the Museum of Contemporary Art, North Miami (opened January 2007), and a trio of exhibitions in 2002 at the Gallery of Fine Art, Edison College, Fort Myers, Florida. A major exhibition curated by Germano Celant was shown at the Fundació Antoni Tàpies in Barcelona (1999), the Fundação de Serralves in Porto (1999), the Museum Moderner Kunst Stiftung Ludwig in Vienna (2000), and the Museo d'Arte Contemporanea, Castello di Rivoli in Turin (2000). The exhibition Five Friends: John Cage, Merce Cunningham, Jasper Johns, Robert Rauschenberg, Cy Twombly, curated by Ron Bishop, was displayed at the Museum Brandhorst (April 10–August 17, 2025) and Museum Ludwig (October 3, 2025–January 11, 2026), with a catalog published in English and German (ISBN 978-3-8296-1043-8). Cunningham choreographed almost 200 works for his company. His visual art was represented by Margarete Roeder Gallery until her death on December 11, 2023.
